experiments.title: Exploratory data analysis
experiments.objective: Characterize the first synthetic dataset (relativistic_dataset_1m.npy) and the held-out extreme_test_10k.npy before modeling.
experiments.config: pandas describe() over 1,000,000 x 13 and 10,000 x 13 arrays
experiments.result: Confirmed the test set spans a much wider beta range (up to 0.999999) than the training set (capped at 0.8).
experiments.observation: The test set is not sampled from the same distribution as training — this is a genuine out-of-distribution / extrapolation setup, not just a held-out split.
experiments.next: Train baseline sklearn regressors on the beta≤ 0.8 training set.

experiments.title: Baseline models on the narrow-range dataset
experiments.objective: Train linear regression, polynomial regression (degree 2-4), decision tree, random forest, extra trees, gradient boosting and hist gradient boosting on relativistic_dataset_1m.npy.
experiments.result: Models fit the training distribution (β ≤ 0.8) reasonably.
experiments.observation: Held out for the next experiment's extrapolation test.
experiments.next: Evaluate all 9 models on the high-beta extreme_test_10k.npy set.

experiments.title: Extrapolation stress test
experiments.objective: Evaluate all 9 era-1 models on extreme_test_10k.npy, whose beta range (up to 0.999999) lies far outside the beta≤ 0.8 training range.
experiments.model: linear regression, polynomial degree 2/3/4, decision tree, random forest, extra trees, gradient boosting, hist gradient boosting
experiments.result: Catastrophic extrapolation failure for most models on most targets: polynomial regression degree 3/4 reach R² as low as -1.7×10⁹; gradient boosting and hist gradient boosting go negative on position, gamma, momentum, kinetic/total energy and proper time. Velocity and beta degrade more gracefully (R² ≈ 0.45-0.50 for most models).
experiments.observation: The notebook's own inline note calls this 'a very interesting result for your research: excellent interpolation but poor extrapolation.' This directly motivated widening the training beta range.
experiments.next: Redesign data generation so the training distribution itself covers the high-beta regime.

experiments.title: Redesigned dataset generation
experiments.objective: Generate physics_data.npy with a beta mixture (70% β∈[0,0.8], 20% β∈[0.8,0.95], 10% β∈[0.95,0.999999]) so training itself spans the relativistic regime, and validate it against the simulator's own consistency checks.
experiments.result: dataset.validate() / manual validation passed: max energy-momentum invariant error 3.2×10⁻¹⁵, all values finite, velocity bound respected.
experiments.observation: Ground truth is exact (closed-form relativistic solution), so all downstream error is attributable to the learned models, not label noise.
experiments.next: Re-train scikit-learn models on the new, wider dataset.

experiments.title: Scikit-learn model sweep on physics_data
experiments.objective: Train 7 scikit-learn regressors on an 800k/100k/100k train/val/test split of physics_data.npy and evaluate on the held-out normal test split.
experiments.model: Linear Regression, Polynomial Degree 2, Decision Tree, Gradient Boosting, Hist Gradient Boosting, Random Forest (controlled), Extra Trees (controlled)
experiments.config: Gradient Boosting: 200 estimators, lr 0.05, max_depth 5; Hist GB: max_iter 200, lr 0.05, max_leaf_nodes 31; Random/Extra Trees: 100 estimators, max_depth 20, min_samples_leaf 10
experiments.result: Hist Gradient Boosting best overall (R² up to 0.99 for position/proper_time); mean R² ranking: Gradient Boosting 0.894 > Hist GB 0.790 > Decision Tree 0.679 > Random Forest 0.654 > Extra Trees 0.652 > Polynomial-2 0.372 > Linear 0.295.
experiments.observation: Gamma remained the hardest target across every model family (best R² 0.98 with Hist GB, but several models under 0.2).
experiments.next: Try neural networks on the same widened dataset, including a normal-vs-extreme comparison.

experiments.title: Feed-forward neural network
experiments.objective: Train a compact fully-connected MLP (5→32→32→32→28→28→24→24→8, 5,536 params) on physics_data.npy and test both on the normal held-out split and on relativistic_extreme_test_10k.npy.
experiments.config: AdamW lr=0.001, weight_decay=1e-5, ReduceLROnPlateau (factor 0.5, patience 3), batch size 4096, 50 epochs, GPU: Tesla T4
experiments.result: Normal test mean R² ≈ 0.72 (proper_time 0.923, position 0.858); extreme test performed comparably (proper_time 0.935, position 0.853) — no meaningful degradation.
experiments.observation: Because era-2 training already spans beta up to 0.999999, the 'extreme' set is no longer a true extrapolation test — it is a comparably-distributed resample, which explains the lack of degradation.
experiments.next: Test whether explicit polynomial feature engineering helps the same architecture.

experiments.title: Degree-2 polynomial-feature neural network
experiments.objective: Expand the 5 input features to 20 (5 linear + 5 squared + 10 pairwise cross terms) and feed them into an MLP of the same depth (20→32→32→32→28→28→24→24→8, 6,016 params).
experiments.config: Same optimizer/scheduler as exp6, but batch size 524,288 (near full-batch), 50 epochs
experiments.result: Substantially worse than the plain MLP: normal test mean R² ≈ 0.29 (gamma R² = -0.042), extreme test similar (≈ 0.31, gamma R² = -0.014). Validation loss was still decreasing at epoch 50 (0.566), unlike the plain MLP which plateaued near 0.21.
experiments.observation: The very large batch size (524,288) sharply reduced the number of gradient updates per epoch, leaving the network under-trained relative to the plain-MLP run — the polynomial features themselves were not tested with a matched training budget.
experiments.next: Consolidate findings into the final comparison and note the confound for future work.
